source: Hart and Staveland (1988) Development of NASA-TLX
finding: Founding paper for the NASA Task Load Index. It built a multidimensional rating scale from several years of work on what makes workload feel different across task types. Six subscales: mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance, effort, frustration. Weights come from the person's own pairwise choices.
numbers: Six subscales; 15 pairwise comparisons for weights (confirmed by a 2025 paper that re-describes the procedure). Original study-level numbers NOT read: the chapter could not be fetched this session (NASA NTRS link 404, host copy not retrievable).
limits: Description taken from a search listing and from later papers, not from the chapter text.
agent_relevance: The agent has no person to rate it. The idea worth keeping: workload has several separable sources, and the weights depend on the task.

source: Pahr and Di Bartolomeo (2025) Investigating the Task Load in Visualization Studies
finding: Describes NASA-TLX as intended: rate six scales, then compare all 15 pairs of scales to get task-specific weights. The weighting step is often dropped, so published TLX scores are hard to compare. Online study of what the full procedure costs participants.
numbers: 34 responses started, 20 complete (long 7, medium 3, short 10). Median TLX questionnaire time 156 s (long) vs 81 s (short). Weighted TLX long 65.29 vs short 50; unweighted RTLX long 51.81 vs short 50. Median frustration 70 (long) vs 40 (short). Average TLX 52.43 vs 43.10.
limits: Very small N (7 vs 10 per arm), volunteers from vis research groups, no demographics. Authors say the weighting procedure itself raises frustration.
agent_relevance: Weighted and raw scores can differ by about 14 points, so the weights are not a minor detail. A single scalar load score hides which source drove it; log sources separately.

source: Pahr and Di Bartolomeo (2025) -- practice of TLX modification
finding: The authors state the weighting step is often omitted because weighted and unweighted scores correlate highly in some studies, but that a raw average can differ greatly from the weighted one in others. So the 'Raw TLX' shortcut is not safe by default.
numbers: Same data as a02: weighted 65.29 against raw 51.81 for the long group, because mental and temporal demand were weighted above frustration, effort and performance.
limits: One task (mini-VLAT visualisation test), n=7 in the long arm.
agent_relevance: If our agent builds a load index from tokens and accuracy, test the weighted and unweighted forms against ground truth rather than assume they agree.

source: Ouwehand, van der Kroef, Wong and Paas (2021) Measuring Cognitive Load: Are There More Valid Alternatives to Likert Rating Scales?
finding: Within-subject test of four rating scales (9-point Likert, 0-100 VAS, emoticons, embodied weights) for perceived difficulty and mental effort on simple and complex weekday problems. The scale that best tracks performance depends on problem complexity.
numbers: N=46 psychology students; 2 (complexity) x 4 (scale) within design; 4 blocks of 4 problems. Scale main effect on mental effort F(1,45)=30.97, ηp2=0.41; on difficulty F=36.45, ηp2=0.45. Complexity effect on effort ηp2=0.96, on difficulty ηp2=0.97. Mean time on task, complex problems: weights 70.77 s, Likert 48.94 s, VAS 43.84 s, emoticons 53.15 s.
limits: Convenience student sample; weekday problems are one narrow task. Best liked: Likert 16, VAS 14, emoticons 13; weights disliked by 26 of 46.
agent_relevance: The measure you pick changes the numbers. A load proxy for the agent should be fixed in advance and validated per task type.

source: Ouwehand et al. (2021) -- rating vs performance correlations
finding: Validity check of each scale against accuracy and time. For complex problems the numeric scales (Likert, VAS) tracked performance: higher rating, lower accuracy, more time. For simple problems the pictorial scales (emoticons, weights) did. Likert detected the link between difficulty and accuracy where the VAS did not.
numbers: Same N=46. Likert, complex problems: accuracy negatively correlated with effort and difficulty; time positively correlated with both. VAS, complex: difficulty not significantly related to accuracy. Pictorial scales: negative links to accuracy and time only for simple problems.
limits: Exact r values are in the paper's Table 5; only sign and significance recorded here. Authors call the pictorial-scale result partial support.
agent_relevance: A subjective scale can be valid in one load regime and blind in another. Do not trust one proxy across easy and hard items.

source: Klepsch, Schmitz and Seufert (2017) Development and Validation of Two Instruments Measuring Intrinsic, Extraneous, and Germane Cognitive Load
finding: Two ways to measure the three load types: trained 'informed' rating of 24 learning situations, and a naive item questionnaire. Both separated high from low load for each type. The germane-load items were the weak point and had to be rewritten.
numbers: Study 1 N=97: informed-rating reliability alpha=0.25 (expected, items measure different things); naive rating alpha ICL=0.86, ECL=0.80, GCL=0.80; high vs low load: informed F(1,89)=293.32, ηp2=0.77; naive F(1,89)=199.96, ηp2=0.69; no difference between methods F(1,89)=1.18, p=0.28. Study 2 (N 65 to 95 per task): alpha ICL 0.81, ECL 0.86, GCL 0.67 (3 items), 0.85 after dropping one item.
limits: Validated by task manipulation, so partly circular. Student self-report. GCL alpha was 0.67 with the item about supporting elements.
agent_relevance: Intrinsic and extraneous load can be rated reliably in humans; germane load cannot be pinned down as well. That supports using only two sources (task difficulty, format noise) in the agent measure.

source: Klepsch et al. (2017) -- structure of the three load types (CFA)
finding: Confirmatory factor analysis compared four models. The paper describes a model with an ECL factor, a broad GCL+ICL factor and a nested ICL-specific factor, which treats intrinsic and germane load as hard to separate.
numbers: Fit criteria used: TLI>=0.95, CFI>=0.95, RMSEA<=0.05, lowest AIC preferred. Study 2 N between 65 and 95 per task.
limits: Per-model fit values are in the paper's table; I did not copy them. Authors still conclude all three load types can be measured.
agent_relevance: Supports a two-way split (what the task needs vs what the format adds) for the agent, in line with the critiques of the three-load model (see subfield 07).

source: Leppink, Paas, Van der Vleuten, Van Gog and Van Merrienboer (2013) Development of an instrument for measuring different types of cognitive load
finding: Ten-item questionnaire for intrinsic, extraneous and germane load. Principal component analysis gave three components; confirmatory analyses on three further cohorts supported it; a randomised experiment gave further support.
numbers: PCA n=56 PhD students; CFA ns=171, 136, 148 bachelor students; randomised experiment n=58 freshmen. Statistics lectures.
limits: Abstract page only (full text paywalled). Later work (Klepsch 2017) found the germane part weaker.
agent_relevance: The standard human route is a three-factor questionnaire validated by factor analysis. Nothing like it exists for a model, so use behaviour, not self-report.

source: Korbach, Brunken and Park (2018) Differentiating Different Types of Cognitive Load: a Comparison of Different Measures
finding: Three-group experiment with extraneous (seductive details), germane (mental animation) and control conditions. The rhythm-method secondary task and subjective ratings both showed higher load in the mental animation group. Eye-tracking Index of Cognitive Activity showed no differences.
numbers: N=78. Mental animation group: higher load by rhythm method and ratings, higher cognitive activity by eye tracking, higher comprehension than the seductive-detail group and higher transfer than control. ICA: no significant differences.
limits: Abstract page only; paywalled.
agent_relevance: Measures disagreed: one physiological index missed what dual-task and ratings caught. Do not pick a single measure; prefer measures anchored to outcomes.

source: DeLeeuw and Mayer (2008) A comparison of three measures of cognitive load
finding: Compared a secondary visual-monitoring reaction-time task, a difficulty rating at the end, and a mental-effort rating, with manipulations aimed at intrinsic, extraneous and germane load. Correlations among the three measures were low and they reacted to different load types, read as support for separable load types.
numbers: Sample sizes and effect sizes not read; full text blocked. Summary comes from a search result describing the paper.
limits: Second-hand description only. Do not quote numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Core reason the field says 'different measures respond to different load types'. Never merge several proxies into one load number without checking.

source: FLoRA Replication Atlas record for DeLeeuw and Mayer (2008)
finding: The atlas lists one replication of DeLeeuw and Mayer (2008), recorded as successful: Zu et al. (2020), using eye movements to measure the three load types. No failed replication is recorded.
numbers: 1 replication on record, 1 successful, earliest 2020. Outcome read by the atlas from the abstract only.
limits: Atlas coverage is partial; absence of a failed replication is not proof none exists. Korbach et al. (2018, a09) found eye tracking (ICA) did not separate groups, which is a tension.
agent_relevance: The measurement claim has one replication, with eye tracking. Thin evidence for a clean measure of each load type.

source: Skulmowski and Rey (2020) Subjective cognitive load surveys lead to divergent results for interactive learning media
finding: Per a later review: subjective load surveys aimed at different kinds of extraneous load (for example verbal vs software-interaction load) lead to different extraneous-load readings, so the survey wording changes the finding.
numbers: No numbers read. Full text behind a Cloudflare block.
limits: Characterisation comes from Skulmowski and Xu (2022, a13), not from the paper itself.
agent_relevance: Wording of the question decides what is measured. Define the agent's measure by operation (tokens, errors), not by a rating label.

source: Skulmowski and Xu (2022) Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load
finding: Review that cites Skulmowski and Rey (2020) as grounds for treating extraneous load as several components. It also records calls to drop germane load and return to a two-part model (Kalyuga 2011; Leppink and van den Heuvel 2015), and notes Sweller (1988) used only intrinsic and extraneous load.
numbers: No new experiment. Cites Paas et al. (2005) for a formula that quantifies motivation as higher load together with higher performance.
limits: Review. The page text had no mention of DeLeeuw and Mayer or NASA-TLX.
agent_relevance: The field is moving toward fewer, better-defined load sources, which fits a design with only task load and format load.

source: Paas and van Merrienboer (1993) The efficiency of instructional conditions: relative condition efficiency
finding: Defines relative condition efficiency: standardise the mental-effort rating and test performance, then take the signed distance from the line where effort equals performance. High performance with low effort counts as efficient.
numbers: Formula as known from the literature: E = (zPerformance - zEffort) / sqrt(2). Not re-derived from the paper; paper not opened.
limits: Needs a population to standardise against; sensitive to the effort scale used (see a04).
agent_relevance: Directly portable. The agent can compute z(accuracy) minus z(tokens) per method across items to rank scaffolds by efficiency, which is the formal model that fits 'use tokens and accuracy'.

source: Paas (1992) Training strategies for attaining transfer of problem-solving skill in statistics
finding: Origin of the single-item 9-point mental-effort rating, from very, very low to very, very high mental effort. Ouwehand et al. (2021) use it as the original 9-point baseline.
numbers: Scale has 9 points. Paas's own numbers not read.
limits: Paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Single-item effort is cheap. The analogue for an agent is total reasoning tokens per item.

source: Kaiser, Frigessi, Ramezani-Kebrya and Ricaud (2025) CogniLoad: A Synthetic Natural Language Reasoning Benchmark
finding: A benchmark built on cognitive load theory with three separate knobs: intrinsic difficulty d, needle-to-hay (distractor) ratio for extraneous load, and task length N as a proxy for germane load. 22 reasoning LLMs were tested. Task length was the dominant stressor.
numbers: 22 models incl. GPT-5 (medium reasoning effort), o3, Gemini 2.5, DeepSeek-R1. Top models degrade slightly d=1 to 3 (o3 0.96 to 0.93; gpt-5 1.00 to 0.97); by d=5, 12 of 22 models are below 50%; gpt-5 0.82 and o3 0.80 at d=10. N=20 to 50: DS-Llama-70B 0.89 to 0.66; Qwen3-8B 0.71 to 0.40. At N=250 only gpt-5 (0.76) and o3 (0.68) are above 50%.
limits: Synthetic state-tracking puzzles. Mapping N onto germane load is the authors' assumption. Max context 32K tokens; default decoding.
agent_relevance: An LLM-side measure by performance: accuracy against each load knob, with 50% capacity thresholds. This is measurement with accuracy, as our subfield note asks.

source: Kaiser et al. (2025) CogniLoad -- U-shaped distractor response
finding: Accuracy was lowest at intermediate distractor ratios (25 to 50 percent needle) and recovered at the extremes for most models. The paper derives 'load capacity' points: the value of one load knob at which predicted accuracy falls to 50 percent.
numbers: gpt-5-mini 0.84 to 0.86; gemini-2.5-flash-lite 0.38 to 0.53; gpt-5 0.97, 0.89, 0.91; o3 0.93, 0.89, 0.88. Weakest: Phi-4-reasoning-plus 0.59 to 0.45; EXAONE-Deep-32B 0.47 to 0.32.
limits: A non-monotonic response means a linear load score would mislead. Capacity figures are model- and puzzle-specific.
agent_relevance: Do not assume more distractors always hurt. Check per-bin, not only a linear trend, when measuring a load-like effect.

source: Kaiser et al. (2025) CogniLoad -- statistical model of capacity
finding: Model form: logit P(correct) = b0 + bd*d + bN*log10(N) + br*r + br2*r^2, fitted per model. In every model d and N are significant and negative. The quadratic distractor term is significant for most models, but not for five (incl. o3, gemini-2.5-pro, gemini-2.5-flash, which are indifferent to distraction).
numbers: Binomial GLM, 22 models, exact-match outcome. Quadratic term gave better AIC in 18 of 22 models.
limits: Coefficient table came out garbled in text extraction, so no coefficient values are recorded.
agent_relevance: A ready recipe: fit per-model logistic curves over a load knob and report the 50 percent threshold. Cheap with tokens and accuracy.

source: Kaiser et al. (2025) CogniLoad -- positioning against long-context benchmarks
finding: States that existing long-context benchmarks (LongBench, L-Eval) vary context length without manipulating intrinsic difficulty, so failures cannot be assigned to a load type. CogniLoad varies each load source on its own.
numbers: Gemini-2.5, gpt-5 and DeepSeek-R1-0528 were run on 10 puzzles per configuration (1,400 instances).
limits: Claim is by the authors. No independent replication found in the sources I opened.
agent_relevance: Methodological rule for our measurement: vary one load source at a time and read accuracy, not self-reports.

source: Shang, Liu, Liang, Zhang, Hu and Guo (2026) United Minds or Isolated Agents? Exploring Coordination of LLMs under Cognitive Load Theory (CoThinker)
finding: Uses CLT as a design lens, not a measurement tool: spread intrinsic load over specialised agents and manage transactional load with structured communication and a shared working memory. Gains concentrate on high-intrinsic-load reasoning tasks; on low-load instruction following, coordination overhead dominates.
numbers: LiveBench and CommonGen-Hard; three Gemini models plus other families; greedy decoding; Holm-corrected paired bootstrap tests, 16 of 25 comparisons significant. Output tokens within 0.89 to 1.11 times MAD. Table 13 deltas for CoThinker: for example +31.2% vs CoT and +123.6% vs MAD in one category; negative in another (about -3.8% to -6.9%).
limits: Load is inferred from task category, not measured on the model. I only partly parsed the per-category table, so relative deltas are approximate and unlabelled by category.
agent_relevance: The authors use a task's cognitive-load profile as a routing signal. This fits our guardrail idea: do not run heavy multi-step machinery on easy items.

source: Figliola, Caputo, Serrano, Mikhaylova, Turchi and Mazzei (2026) Neither Replacement nor Panacea: LLM conversational vs graphical decision support
finding: Human-subject study using raw (unweighted) NASA-TLX as the workload measure for an LLM interface. The chat interface lowered perceived workload overall and was faster on easy tasks, but the advantage shrank as task complexity rose. No consistent accuracy advantage.
numbers: 134 industrial decision makers, 2x3 mixed design. TLX rose with complexity: T2 vs T1 beta=0.415, T3 vs T1 beta=1.536, T3 vs T2 beta=1.121, omnibus LR=127.302, p<.001. Predicted accuracy 0.894 (T1), 0.846 (T2), 0.488 (T3). Chatbot faster on T1 by 37.0 s. Data literacy did not moderate (LR=4.152, p=.125).
limits: Raw TLX only, no pairwise weights; self-report. Measures the human's load, not the model's.
agent_relevance: In a field setting TLX moved with task complexity while accuracy fell, so rating and performance can be read together. The size of the effect depends on the interface.

source: Pahr and Di Bartolomeo (2025) -- what the weights add
finding: Physical demand was consistently rated unimportant and had no effect on the long-version score, but dragged the short-version score down. Mental and temporal demand were weighted higher on average than frustration, effort and performance.
numbers: Weighted TLX 65.29 vs raw 51.81 in the long arm (n=7).
limits: n=7. Single task.
agent_relevance: Dimensions that do not apply to a task should be dropped or they bias the average. For the agent, drop irrelevant proxies.

source: Ouwehand et al. (2021) -- design and power
finding: Planned for f=0.25, power 0.95, alpha 0.05, which needs at least 23 participants; 46 took part. Each scale was used in a block of four problems, with block order varied across participants.
numbers: N=46; 4 blocks of 4 problems; ηp2 benchmarks 0.01 small, 0.06 medium, 0.14 large.
limits: Within-subject design compares scales directly but carries order effects.
agent_relevance: A template for a within-item comparison of our own proxies across scaffolds.

source: Zu et al. (2020) Using eye movements to measure intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load in a multimedia learning environment
finding: Recorded by the replication atlas as replicating the main results of DeLeeuw and Mayer and supporting the triarchic structure, using eye movements.
numbers: No numbers. Abstract sentence only, via the atlas record (a11).
limits: Page not fetched (paywalled). Sits in tension with Korbach et al. (2018), where the eye-tracking index did not separate groups.
agent_relevance: Treat the eye-movement route as unsettled.

source: Hart and Staveland (1988) -- reliability and sensitivity claims (not verified)
finding: Placeholder: the chapter could not be read, so no reliability or sensitivity numbers are recorded rather than invented. Next step: open the NASA Ames scanned PDF and extract experiment counts, the between-rater variability reduction from weighting, and test-retest r.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Missing source text.
agent_relevance: None until opened.
